The role of a 'reflector' or self-critique step is explored in both Mobile-Agent-v3 and MobileUse, with some agreement on its fundamental function but divergence on its optimal application. In Mobile-Agent-v3, the Reflector Agent is a critical component for ensuring robustness and learning from mistakes [DOC 1]. The 2024-2026 multi-agent literature presents several recurring arguments for and against utilizing multi-agent systems over a single, stronger Large Language Model (LLM). A primary argument in favor of multi-agent systems is their ability to extend the capabilities and application domain of single LLM-based agent systems, particularly in areas like software engineering and automating research (Zhang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024b) [DOC 0]. Proponents argue that the collective intelligence derived from a group of specialized agents can yield better results than relying on a single agent (Hong et al. 2023) [DOC 0]. Multi-agent frameworks represent a key trend in the development of LLM-driven agents [DOC 2].

Furthermore, multi-agent systems are posited to overcome a fundamental problem: the capability overload of a single policy network [DOC 2]. Coupling heterogeneous abilities, such as high-level strategic planning with low-level visual perception and precise execution, into the same model inevitably leads to optimization conflicts and role confusion [DOC 2]. Multi-agent systems address this by innovating through architecture, thoroughly decoupling different responsibilities to enhance all facets of the agent’s capabilities via specialized division of labor and collaboration [DOC 2]. This specialized division of labor and intelligent collaboration allows multi-agent systems to overcome the inherent limitations of single agents in handling complex, dynamic, and long-horizon tasks [DOC 2]. For example, multi-agent architectures integrate LLMs to overcome the constraints inherent to using standalone LLMs in hardware design [DOC 3].

Conversely, significant arguments against multi-agent systems revolve around security and operational challenges. Strongly interacting networks of autonomous agents pose novel security problems that are poorly understood and could constitute systemic risks (OpenAI 2024a) [DOC 4]. A specific vulnerability identified is the "Multi-Agent Security Tax," which involves the propagation of malicious prompts within multi-agent LLM systems, analogous to worms in traditional digital systems [DOC 0, DOC 4]. Beyond security, the literature also highlights practical concerns such as the computational costs associated with multi-agent approaches, which raise environmental concerns regarding energy consumption [DOC 9].
